Notes

Liver Surgical Anatomy

COUINAUD SEGMENTS I–VIII
Liver surgery depends on precise segmental anatomy — wrong orientation/identification → major vascular injury/bleeding. Each of the 8 segments is an anatomical unit requiring all four of the following:
RequirementStructure
Portal venous inflowPortal vein
Hepatic arterial inflowHepatic artery
Venous outflowHepatic vein
Biliary drainageBile duct
Same principle in transplantation/lobar grafts: the graft fails if any one of these four is missing.
PRINGLE MANEUVER
Occlusion/compression of the portal vein + hepatic artery → stops hepatic inflow.
BLEEDING DESPITE PRINGLE
Persistent bleeding → think retrograde bleeding from hepatic veins/IVC — the source is not portal/arterial inflow.
  • Structure not in the portal triad → hepatic vein (triad = portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct). 438 ×2
Notes

Functional Reserve

Resection requires assessment of functional reserve, not merely anatomical liver volume.

LiverTolerance of Resection
Healthy liverCan tolerate major resection (~70%)
Cirrhotic/injured liverMay look large yet have very poor reserve → even small resection can cause post-hepatectomy liver failure
Decompensated cirrhosisGenerally not suitable for hepatic resection
Notes

Benign Liver Masses

Primary liver masses are broadly benign vs malignant; metastatic liver disease is a separate topic.

Notes

At a Glance

FeatureHemangiomaFNHHepatic Adenoma
NatureMost common benign tumor (~5%); vascular/blood-filledHyperplasia of otherwise normal hepatocytesPremalignant; OCP/hormone- associated
Key imagingPeripheral → centripetal fill-in; T2 very brightCentral scar with radiating spokes ("orange segments")May be hard to distinguish from early HCC
Malignant potentialNoneNone→ HCC; also rupture/hemorrhage
BiopsyAvoid — bleeding, non-diagnosticUnnecessary — shows normal liver—
Management HemangiomaUsually observeUsually no treatmentStop OCP → observe ≤1 yr → persistent → surgery
Usually incidental and requires no treatment. Degenerative changes may make imaging atypical → further imaging.
US→Multiphasic CT→MRI if diagnosis still doubtful
DO NOT BIOPSY ROUTINELY
Vascular lesion → bleeding risk; sampling may be non-diagnostic (adjacent normal liver or only blood).

Multiphasic CT Phases

PhaseContrast Location
Non-contrastNo contrast in aorta
ArterialPredominantly in aorta/arterial system
Portal venousPortal system/liver enhances after blood returns from bowel/spleen
DelayedContrast drains through hepatic veins
Typical Hemangioma Imaging
Peripheral enhancement→Progressive centripetal fill-in→Delayed complete filling
MRI
T1 → dark · T2 → very bright · contrast shows the same peripheral → central fill-in. Used when degenerative changes disturb the CT pattern.
INDICATIONS FOR SURGERY
Symptoms — subcapsular lesion stretching Glisson capsule
Documented progressive enlargement
Mass effect: duodenum/gastric outlet, stomach, diaphragm
WHY PAIN?
Liver parenchyma has little pain sensation — symptoms arise mainly from capsular stretching.
★ OSCE / EXAM PATTERN
Young woman + persistent RUQ pain + liver lesion on US → multiphasic CT → peripheral enhancement → centripetal filling → delayed complete filling = hemangioma. Symptomatic + subcapsular → capsular stretching explains pain → intervention may be considered. Professor stated this pattern may appear as an OSCE image question.
  • Peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in → haemangioma. 442
Notes

Focal Nodular Hyperplasia (FNH)

BENIGN — NO MALIGNANT TRANSFORMATION
Localized hyperplasia (increased number of otherwise normal hepatocytes). Diagnosis by US/CT/MRI; classic central scar with radiating spokes. Biopsy shows essentially normal liver → unnecessary when imaging is characteristic. Usually no treatment; intervene mainly for significant symptoms or progressive enlargement.
  • Hypervascular lesion with a central stellate scar → FNH 442; incidental 3-cm FNH → no treatment needed. 438 ×2
Notes

Hepatic Adenoma

PREMALIGNANT — THREE DANGERS
Spontaneous rupture · hemorrhage · malignant transformation → HCC. Adenoma and HCC are the key liver masses capable of spontaneous rupture/bleeding.
Adenoma suspected woman on OCP→Stop OCP immediately→Observe ≤ ~1 year may regress/disappear→Persistent → surgery
ADENOMA VS EARLY HCC
CT/MRI may be unable to confidently distinguish adenoma from early HCC → operative management may be required.
  • OCP user, incidental arterially enhancing mass → stop OCPs, repeat imaging in 6 months 441; adenoma not regressing 6 months after stopping OCP → surgical resection. 442 ×3
Notes

Liver Cysts

Cystic lesions discussed:

Simple liver cyst Polycystic disease Hydatid cyst

Multiple simple cysts
Biliary cyst
  • Cyst that can look like a solid mass on CT → hydatid cyst (degenerated/calcified type). 438
  • Most serious complication of hepatic hydatid disease → anaphylaxis (rupture/spillage). 429
Notes

Simple Cyst

Contains serous fluid; single or multiple; can become very large. Large/subcapsular → capsular stretching → pain.

NEEDLE ASPIRATION — NOT DEFINITIVE
Fluid reaccumulates, and it introduces risk of infection → liver abscess.
PREFERRED: LAPAROSCOPIC DEROOFING/FENESTRATION
Remove the free/exposed wall ("remove the hat") and leave the cyst open → fluid drains and is absorbed rather than reaccumulating.

Multiple cysts do not automatically need treatment — confirm symptoms truly come from the cyst; treat selected symptomatic cysts, not every lesion.

  • Amoebic liver abscess (positive E. histolytica serology) → initial antiamoebic drugs (metronidazole). 429 ×2
Notes

Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)

Primary malignant tumors discussed: HCC, cholangiocarcinoma, and fibrolamellar tumor (HCC variant in younger patients).

  • Egyptian man with bilharziasis → HCC risk (schistosomiasis + HCV co-infection). 427 ×2
  • Paraneoplastic syndromes of HCC — all except → keyed hyperglycaemia (HCC causes hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, erythrocytosis). 426
Notes

Risk Factors

BACKGROUND: CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE/CIRRHOSIS
The cirrhotic liver is a "fertile field" — it can produce further HCC even after complete resection.

Viral hepatitis

Metabolic liver disease
Copper-storage disorders

Alcohol

Iron-storage disorders
IMPORTANT DISTINCTION
HBV can cause HCC even without established cirrhosis.
  • Weakest association with HCC (smoker on HRT with HBV + HCV) → OCP/hormones 436; all predispose except → keyed smoking (least risk; hepatitis A causes no chronic disease). 426
  • HBV cirrhosis, jaundice and weight loss, hypervascular mass → confirm with α-fetoprotein. 426
Notes

Clinical Features & Spread

May present through the underlying liver disease (decompensation/ascites).

RouteDetails
LocalSatellite lesions around the primary mass
VascularVenous/tumor thrombus
LungHepatic veins → IVC → heart → lungs
BoneVertebral metastases → spinal symptoms/compression
BrainAlso discussed
AFP
Α-FETOPROTEIN
Elevated in ~70%; ~30% remain negative.
FOLLOW-UP RULE
A tumor marker is useful for follow-up only if elevated at baseline. Normal AFP from the start → unreliable for that patient (same principle as CEA in colorectal cancer).
  • "All are liver cysts except" → metastasis (from colon cancer is solid). 426
  • Pyogenic liver abscess with Streptococcus faecalis (gut organism) → spread via the portal route. 426
Notes

HCC Diagnosis

US→Multiphasic/triphasic CT→MRI if CT equivocal

MRI has higher sensitivity but is more time-consuming and vulnerable to patient movement and claustrophobia — CT remains practical and widely used.

★ Classic HCC Imaging (Cirrhotic Liver)
Arterial phase early hyperenhancement+Portal/delayed phase washout=Classic HCC ★★★
EXAM QUESTION — ENHANCEMENT + WASHOUT
Must show enhancement and washout in the same lesion/location. Arterial enhancement without washout may be another vascular phenomenon such as a shunt, not classic HCC.

Biopsy — the HCC Exception

SettingBiopsy?
General oncologyTissue usually required — "no tissue, no issue"
Cirrhotic + classic enhancement + washoutNot required — radiological diagnosis
Non-cirrhotic or atypical imagingRequired
Prognostic Factors
Worse prognosis with: • Larger tumor size • Bilobar vs one lobe • Underlying cirrhosis • Aggressive tumor biology• Multiple vs solitary • Extrahepatic spread • Poor performance status • Vascular/lymphovascular involvement
RECURRENCE
Even after R0 resection, the cirrhotic background can produce new HCC.
Classic HCC (cirrhotic liver): arterial-phase hyperenhancement + washout in the portal/delayed phase — in the same lesion. No biopsy needed in a cirrhotic with classic imaging (biopsy if non-cirrhotic or atypical).
  • HCV cirrhosis, 2-cm lesion with early arterial enhancement and early washout → HCC. 439 ×5
Notes

HCC Treatment

TREATMENT DEPENDS ON BOTH
1. Tumor burden/biology + 2. Underlying liver function.
Notes

Liver Transplant

Major advantage: treats both the HCC and the cirrhotic liver that produced it. Not every patient is eligible — recurrence rises markedly with excessive tumor burden.

★ MILAN CRITERIA
Single tumor <5 cm
OR
≤3 tumors, each <3 cm
→ acceptable recurrence risk → transplant candidate.
EXTENDED CRITERIA
Solitary lesion up to ~6.5 cm, provided no major lymphovascular invasion, lymph-node disease, or extrahepatic disease. Larger tumors → higher recurrence; allocation must consider expected outcome.
★ EXAM SCENARIO
Cirrhotic patient + single HCC ~4–4.8 cm, otherwise within criteria → liver transplant. While waiting → bridging locoregional therapy to prevent progression beyond criteria.
Milan criteria → transplant: single tumour < 5 cm, or ≤ 3 tumours each < 3 cm (extended: solitary up to ~6.5 cm without vascular/nodal/extrahepatic disease). Bridge with locoregional therapy while waiting.
  • 4-cm HCC with Child B cirrhosis → liver transplant. 438 ×5
Notes

Liver Resection

GOOD OPTION WHEN
Liver function preserved
Patient can physiologically tolerate surgery Very cirrhotic/decompensated liver → poor candidate.
ADVANTAGES OVER TRANSPLANT
Retains native liver
Avoids lifelong immunosuppression + complications
Transplant remains an option later

Child-Pugh Concept

Estimates hepatic functional reserve; parameters mentioned: albumin, bilirubin, INR, ascites.

ClassScoreLecture Treatment Framing
Child A5–6Preserved function → potentially suitable for definitive local/resection therapy
Child B7–9Especially 7–8 → consider locoregional therapy; 9 relatively advanced
Child C10–15Severe decompensation → invasive/resection/locoregional treatment generally poorly tolerated
Locoregional Treatment
TechniqueMechanismBest Use
RFANeedle into tumor → heat → protein denaturation/coagulative destructionSmall lesions ≤3 cm; high-risk/elderly patients. A 4 cm lesion may exceed one standard zone → overlapping needles
CryotherapyExtreme cold (liquid nitrogen) → protein denaturation/cell destructionBoth extreme heat and cold denature proteins
Ethanol injectionAbsolute alcohol (~99%) into tumorOlder technique, before modern RFA/TACE
TACESuper-selective arterial catheterization → chemotherapy → embolization (retains drug, cuts arterial supply)Larger lesions (e.g. ~12 cm → TACE, not RFA); bridging to transplant
RadioembolizationIntra-arterial radioactive particles → radiation from within the lesion Assessing Response After Embolization/AblationLarger tumors
NO ENHANCEMENT ON CONTRAST CT
No viable perfused tumor → successful devascularization.
RESIDUAL/NEW ENHANCEMENT
Viable tumor, revascularization, or incomplete treatment.

Response is judged by residual enhancement/viable tissue, not lesion size alone.

Notes

Gross Appearance of Liver Tumors

TumorGross Appearance
HemangiomaCut surface resembles a sponge/vascular spaces
HCCRelatively soft; can undergo necrosis and rupture/bleed
CholangiocarcinomaClassically very hard/solid; capsular retraction
Notes

Cholangiocarcinoma & Caroli Disease

CHOLANGIOCARCINOMA
Malignant tumor of biliary epithelium; intrahepatic lesions are grossly hard with capsular retraction.

Choledochal cysts are classified as types I–V.

Type V = Caroli disease→Intrahepatic strictures + dilatations→Stasis → intrahepatic stones·Cholangiocarcinoma

Lecture example: a young patient with Caroli disease, intrahepatic stones and cholangiocarcinoma.

  • Cholangiocarcinoma is most common at the bifurcation of the hepatic ducts (Klatskin tumour). 426
Notes

TIPS

TRANSJUGULAR INTRAHEPATIC PORTOSYSTEMIC SHUNT
Stent creating an intrahepatic connection between the portal vein and hepatic venous/systemic circulation → reduces portal pressure, especially in severe portal-hypertension-related bleeding from cirrhosis. At transplantation, the diseased liver and its TIPS stent may be removed together.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 Every liver segment/graft needs portal inflow + arterial inflow + venous outflow + biliary drainage
2 Pringle = occlude portal vein + hepatic artery; bleeding continues → hepatic vein/IVC source
3 Resection depends on functional reserve, not volume — healthy liver tolerates ~70%; decompensated cirrhosis → no resection
4 Hemangioma: most common benign tumor; peripheral → centripetal fill-in; T1 dark/T2 very bright; avoid biopsy
5 Hemangioma surgery only for symptoms (subcapsular capsular stretch), progressive growth, or mass effect
6 FNH: central scar with radiating spokes, benign, no malignant transformation, usually no biopsy/treatment
7 Adenoma: OCP-associated, rupture/bleeding + HCC transformation → stop OCP, observe ≤1 year, persistent → surgery
8 Simple cyst: aspiration is not definitive (recurrence + abscess) → laparoscopic deroofing/fenestration
9 HCC arises on cirrhosis ("fertile field"), but HBV can cause HCC without cirrhosis
10 AFP raised in ~70%; a marker only helps follow-up if it was elevated at baseline
11 Classic HCC = arterial hyperenhancement + portal/delayed washout in the same lesion ★★★
12 Cirrhotic liver + classic imaging → no biopsy needed; non-cirrhotic or atypical → biopsy
13 Milan: 1 lesion <5 cm OR ≤3 lesions each <3 cm → transplant; bridge with locoregional therapy while waiting
14 Child A → resection candidate; Child B (7–8) → locoregional; Child C → treatments poorly tolerated
15 RFA for small lesions (≤3 cm); large tumors (e.g. 12 cm) → TACE or radioembolization
16 After ablation/embolization: no enhancement = non-viable tumor; enhancement = residual viable disease
17 Cholangiocarcinoma = hard tumor with capsular retraction; Caroli (type V) → intrahepatic stones + cholangiocarcinoma risk
18 TIPS = transjugular portal → hepatic vein stent to lower portal pressure in portal-hypertensive bleeding
